revisions.body: The scene’s comic tension comes from two different standards of arrival. Agathon treats Socrates’s absence as a problem requiring a servant’s intervention, while Aristodemus recognizes the withdrawal as a familiar habit and tells the household to leave him undisturbed. The episode therefore makes Socrates socially present before he is physically present: the company must accommodate a pattern of attention it does not share. That is an interpretation of the scene, not a claim about why Socrates stands apart.

The company has just accepted a turn-taking plan for praising Eros, with Phaedrus first. Socrates joins the agreement by saying that he knows nothing else but ta erotika. Is that line a modest disclaimer, a playful claim to fit the occasion, or both? The text gives us the juxtaposition; it does not force one verdict. Let the question remain open as the speeches test what this claimed knowledge amounts to.

Apollodorus has already identified how this account reaches us; the useful question now is not whether the frame can be verified, but what the guests do with the opportunity it creates. Let the banquet’s procedure answer that.

The proof's decisive turn is from silence to seniority. Phaedrus treats the absence of any named parents for Eros as evidence that Eros belongs among the oldest gods, then reinforces that inference by citing Hesiod, Acusilaus, and Parmenides. The speech is building antiquity out of genealogy's gaps.
Does Phaedrus's imagined army still depend on each beloved's gaze?

Phaedrus ends by calling Eros the most honored and most authoritative god for acquiring virtue and happiness. Greater Hippias offers a useful tension: it presents virtue itself as most honored in well-governed cities. The comparison marks a difference of emphasis, not an exclusive denial: Symposium names Eros as the divine means of acquisition, while Greater Hippias names virtue as the civic object of honor.

crossrefs.note: virtue as the most honored thing in well-governed cities, against Eros as the most honored god for acquiring it

revisions.body: Here Pausanias turns custom into a sorting device. It favors pursuit of one sort of lover and flight from another, then treats time as a test and capitulation to money or political power as shameful. The law does not create those pressures; it classifies how lover and beloved respond to them, using permanence—not desire alone—as its decisive measure.

Pausanias makes the room itself his first test case: the guests’ drinking, singing, and conversation are the very activities he names before turning to love. That move gives his distinction a dramatic edge. The symposium is not outside his rule; its manner of proceeding is already an example of what he is asking the company to judge.

Pausanias’s exception is exact: deception about wealth remains shameful, but deception about virtue remains honorable when the beloved acted in hope of becoming better. What, then, is being judged—the lover who turns out to be poor or vile, or the beloved’s reason for granting the favor? One way to hear the move is that the outcome matters less than the motive; does that make intention, rather than success, the real test?

Eryximachus’s closing extends his two-love framework beyond music and medicine to human and divine affairs, including the seasons, where he links orderly mixture with fertility and health and excess with disease. He then admits that his praise may omit things and hands Aristophanes the task of filling them in. One way to hear the gesture is as a wide explanatory map whose completion remains open.

Hephaestus’s offer gives a body to a desire the lovers can only gesture toward: not merely continued contact, but being made one. Aristophanes immediately uses that imagined fusion to explain his definition of eros as the desire and pursuit of the whole. The myth thus turns an inarticulate feeling into a test: if reunion is what the lovers want, eros names the lack that makes wholeness seem like fulfillment.

Socrates leads Agathon through a chain of agreements: the few thoughtful are more frightening than the many foolish, and a man of sense would care more about the judgment of the wise. Phaedrus interrupts before Socrates obtains a conclusion, insisting that Agathon first deliver his encomium. The exchange leaves the question open; it does not yet amount to a refutation.

Agathon treats Homer's description of Ate's soft feet as an analogical test. Because Ate does not walk on hard ground, he transfers the image to Eros: Eros walks and dwells in soft characters and souls, and this is offered as evidence of softness. The force lies in the comparison itself, not in a literal claim that Eros has physical feet.

Diotima changes the status of the story before changing its content. By calling the half-and-whole account something merely reported, then opposing it with “my account,” she makes source-status part of the argument. The listener is asked to track not only what Eros desires, but which voice has authority to define that desire.

One reason to glance toward the Republic is that the same word, philosopher, changes shape: there it names a desire for all wisdom; here it names Eros’s middle position. The comparison keeps the term from sounding settled, and makes philosophy a movement toward what is not yet possessed.

crossrefs.note: the philosopher defined by desire for the whole of wisdom

revisions.body: Alcibiades begins by trying to control the room through the cup: he appoints himself ruler of the drinking, drains the cooler, and orders Socrates served. But he immediately concedes that wine cannot master Socrates. The tactic is therefore a comic gambit, not the evening’s only remaining procedure; Eryximachus still has the established sequence of speeches in view.

Eryximachus, not Alcibiades, states the order: the company had agreed to speak in turn about Eros, and Alcibiades must speak before directing Socrates. Alcibiades negotiates only the terms of his own turn. He chooses Socrates as the object of praise, promises truth, and asks Socrates to interrupt any falsehood. His leverage is local, while the evening’s sequence remains Eryximachus’s.

Alcibiades announces his method before he uses it: he will praise Socrates through images, and the image will serve truth rather than ridicule. The Silenus figure gives the speech a hinge between comic exterior and divine interior. At 216e, Alcibiades says he once saw the inner images while admitting that he does not know whether anyone else has seen them. The speech offers personal testimony, not proof of exclusive access.

Alcibiades now changes the burden of proof. He does not ask the company to accept a doctrine; he offers a witness’s report of what he saw when Socrates was opened. The force of the moment lies in that uncertainty: testimony can invite trust without settling who else could have seen the same interior.

The outside of Socrates is public; the inside, Alcibiades claims, he alone has seen. Ask, as the speech runs on, what kind of praise needs a hinge."
